attachments.title: Source clinical note
attachments.text:
ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2020-07-15
Provider: Dr. Michael Rodriguez, MD
Department: Pediatrics
Visit Type: inpatient

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Fever and a widespread rash

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient is a 5-year-old male with a history of underimmunization and respiratory diphtheria diagnosed in January 2020 who presents for inpatient management following an outpatient pediatrics evaluation earlier today for worsening symptoms. His mother reports that he began feeling unwell about 4 days ago, starting with a low-grade fever, runny nose, and a mild cough. Over the next two days, his symptoms worsened—he developed red, watery eyes and became increasingly tired, spending much of the day lying on the couch and refusing to eat. This morning, she noticed that he had a red blotchy rash behind his ears, which quickly spread over his face and neck. By the time they arrived at the hospital, the rash had extended to his chest, abdomen, and arms. His mother also points out that she saw some tiny white spots inside his mouth while trying to give him water.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Respiratory diphtheria (Pharyngeal diphtheria) (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Measles (wild-type) (diagnosed 2020-07-15)
- Underimmunization
- Iron deficiency anemia

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- None

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Ferrous sulfate 6 mg/kg elemental iron daily
- Multivitamin with vitamin A 1 chewable tablet daily

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
- Father: healthy, vaccine hesitant
- Mother: healthy, vaccine hesitant
- Younger sister: healthy, underimmunized

SOCIAL HISTORY:
The family recently moved into a new apartment after living in a transitional shelter. The boy had previously attended preschool regularly, but he has not been enrolled in a new one yet due to the relocation. His mother says that she has been trying to rebuild stability for both of them after completing a 6-month inpatient program for amphetamine use disorder. She now participates in weekly counseling and attends parenting classes. She is worried that her son may have caught something from other children at the shelter, but she isn't sure when he last saw a pediatrician. She has not noticed any recent travel, no known tick exposure, and no one else in the apartment currently has a rash.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:
The child has had no seizures, vomiting, or changes in consciousness.

VITAL SIGNS:
Temperature of 39.4°C (102.9°F), heart rate mildly elevated

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On exam, the boy appears fatigued. He has a mild cough and thin nasal discharge. His conjunctivae are injected bilaterally, and there are multiple small, bluish-white lesions on an erythematous base along his buccal mucosa. His breath sounds are clear. Skin examination reveals a diffuse, erythematous, maculopapular rash that began at the head and is now spreading down the neck and trunk, with some confluence noted on the face and upper chest. The rash is non-vesicular and blanches with pressure. There is no lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, or evidence of skin peeling.

ENCOUNTER NOTE
Date: 2020-01-15
Provider: Dr. Sarah Chen, MD
Department: Emergency Medicine
Visit Type: ed

CHIEF COMPLAINT:
Difficulty swallowing, sore throat, and low-grade fever for the past 2 days

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
His mother reports that he has been increasingly lethargic and has refused to eat. There is no history of cough or rhinorrhea.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
Active Problem List:
- Underimmunization
- Iron deficiency anemia

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:
- None

MEDICATIONS:
Home Medications:
- Ferrous sulfate 6 mg/kg elemental iron daily
- Multivitamin with vitamin A 1 chewable tablet daily

ALLERGIES:
No known drug allergies

FAMILY HISTORY:
His younger sibling at home is currently healthy.

SOCIAL HISTORY:
He recently immigrated to the United States

VITAL SIGNS:
He has a temperature of 38.2°C (100.8°F).

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:
On physical examination, the child appears ill. Oropharyngeal inspection reveals a thick, grayish membrane coating the tonsils and posterior pharynx that bleeds when attempts are made to dislodge it. Bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy and mild neck swelling are noted. Cardiopulmonary and neurologic examinations are unremarkable.

LABORATORY DATA:
A nasopharyngeal swab is sent for culture and toxin assay

PLAN:
The patient is started on empiric antibiotic therapy and antitoxin.
